cards.back: Know the WHOLE play, not just the extracts — context matters for every question.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Set Text Analysis and Exam Preparation
cards.back: Extract questions: analyse the specific scene AND connect it to the whole play's themes and structure.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Set Text Analysis and Exam Preparation
cards.back: Three perspectives: you may be asked from performer, director or designer viewpoint — always answer from the specified perspective.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Set Text Analysis and Exam Preparation
cards.back: Structure your answer: point (identify technique/choice) + evidence (specific reference) + explanation (effect on audience) + link (to whole play themes).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Set Text Analysis and Exam Preparation
cards.back: Time management: Section A is 45 minutes — plan for 5 minutes, write for 35 minutes, check for 5 minutes.

cards.front: What should you know about drama exam tips?
cards.back: For the written exam, use the SEE framework for each point: State your choice (e.g. 'I would position the character DS centre'), Evidence from the text ('because at this moment they are confronting the truth'), Effect on audience ('creating maximum focus and intimacy'), Link to theme ('which reflects the play's central theme of honesty').
Close reading of set passage (e.g. 20-25 mins)
Apply theory to specific text (e.g. 15-20 mins)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: For the written exam, you just need to learn the story of the play and describe what happens in the extract. Correct: The written exam tests your ABILITY TO REALISE the text, not just recall the plot. As a performer, describe how you would use vocal and physical skills to realise a key moment in the given extract. Justify your choices with reference to the whole play.

The set text exam (Component 1, Section A) tests AO1 (knowledge), AO2 (analysis), and AO3 (performance application). You must know the play in depth AND be able to make specific performance/design/directorial choices. Questions always specify a perspective — performer, director or designer — and your answer must match. The mark scheme rewards precision, justification and whole-play understanding.

GCSE set text analysis requires a systematic approach that uncovers how the playwright creates meaning through structure, character, language and theatrical devices. Begin with an overview: what is the play about (theme), who is it about (character), and what happens (plot)? GCSE Drama set text questions typically fall into three categories: extract-based questions (analysing a specific section of the text), whole-play questions (evaluating a theme or character across the entire play), and performance questions (proposing how a section could be staged or performed).
